title: Can woolly bear caterpillars predict winter?
description: A woolly bear’s black and rusty bands look like a tiny weather chart. Discover what they really reveal, and why sensing weather is different from forecasting winter.

cover.alt: A black-ended, rusty-brown woolly bear caterpillar on an autumn leaf beside a fallen log
cover.credit: AI-generated realistic illustration created for BrainiLab; an imagined caterpillar scene, not a documented specimen or weather observation.

sections.title: A tiny weather chart?
sections.html:
A woolly bear caterpillar’s coloured bands do not reliably predict how harsh the coming winter will be. The familiar claim is folklore: more black supposedly means a harder winter, while a wider rusty middle promises a milder one.

It makes an appealing outdoor guessing game. But the US National Weather Service explains why the bands are not a winter forecast.

sections.title: A record of growing
sections.html:
A caterpillar’s colouring reflects factors such as its age, feeding and species. As woolly bears grow and shed their skins, their colouring changes. Two different-looking caterpillars need not be issuing different predictions.

The useful twist is about time: the bands tell us about the animal’s growth, rather than weather that has not happened yet.

sections.title: Finding a winter address
sections.html:
A woolly bear crossing a path in autumn is looking for a sheltered place to spend winter, such as under bark or a fallen log. Its direction is not a secret forecast either.

For the larger seasonal story, see why summer is warmer than winter. Preparing for a season and predicting its severity are different things.

sections.title: Sensing weather is a different skill
sections.html:
Animals can still notice real changes. The Hong Kong Observatory describes birds sensing air pressure and infrasound, which can help them respond to approaching weather. That is different from reading a whole winter from a caterpillar’s coat.

Even scientific seasonal forecasts describe probabilities, not a guaranteed sequence of days, as the Met Office explains.

The woolly bear remains worth noticing. Its bands offer a clue to its own life, not a weather chart for yours.
